books.section: Topic 4.3 Politics and Regional Interests, C. A Temporary Truce on the Slavery Question in the Pre-Civil War Period

stimulus.text: An abolitionist wall map of the United States, published in the 1850s, colors free states and slave states differently and draws a line across the western territories labeled as the Missouri Compromise line. The territories beyond the line are marked as lands “whose destiny is yet to be decided.”
stimulus.source_note: Map of the United States, showing by colors the area of freedom and slavery, published 1850s (abolitionist wall map; scan of pre-1930 original). Public domain.

source: original; stimulus is an 1850s abolitionist wall map showing the Missouri Compromise line (public domain, in the shared image pool as 5s24-ch14-mcq-01)
stem: The map’s label for the western territories, “whose destiny is yet to be decided,” best reflects the idea that

options.text: slavery in the West was still undecided and would be fought over again
the West had no settlers and no government at all in the 1850s
options.misconception: Western territories had settlers and territorial governments by the 1850s; undecided means the slavery question, not emptiness.

options.text: Congress had already decided the fate of every western territory
options.misconception: That is what “yet to be decided” denies; the label says the fate is still open.

options.text: the mapmaker supported the spread of slavery into the West
options.misconception: An abolitionist mapmaker opposed slavery’s spread; the map argues against it, not for it.

rationales.A: “Yet to be decided” means the slavery question in the West was still open. The mapmaker knew the Compromise line had only postponed the fight, and the 1850s proved him right.
rationales.B: The territories were not empty. They had settlers, towns, and territorial governments. What was undecided was whether slavery would follow the settlers.
rationales.C: “Yet to be decided” is the opposite of decided. Congress had drawn one line in 1820 and was still arguing over the West thirty years later.
rationales.D: This is an abolitionist map, made to show slavery as a spreading stain. Its maker wanted slavery stopped, not spread.
rationales.general:
1. Read the label literally. “Whose destiny is yet to be decided” means the outcome is still open.
2. Ask which destiny. The map is about freedom and slavery, so the question is whether slavery spreads west.
3. Ask what the mapmaker expects. He colors a line drawn in 1820 and still argues about it in the 1850s.
4. Put it together. The label says the Compromise postponed the fight, not ended it.
Background: by the 1850s the Kansas-Nebraska Act had repealed the line, and the West was again the center of the slavery fight.
Remember: “yet to be decided” is a claim about the future, so ask what fight is still coming.
